passage: Uday here. I was standing by the water cooler when a boy from the other class started tapping Harsha's head with a ruler again. Harsha had been quiet for weeks, and I expected him to freeze. Instead he looked straight at the boy and said, "Stop that. I don't like it." His voice wobbled a little, but it did not shout. Then he picked up his bottle and walked off towards the staff room. I heard later that he had told the class teacher earlier that week and had practised those words with them. I can't say if he was scared inside. The ruler boy just stood there with his mouth open, and that afternoon the class teacher had a word with him.

qa.q: What did Harsha say to the boy with the ruler?
qa.a: He said, "Stop that. I don't like it."

qa.q: What might Harsha have been feeling as he spoke, judging by his wobbling voice?
qa.a: He was probably nervous, but Uday cannot be sure; the wobble alongside steady words suggests he was brave even though he may have been afraid.

qa.q: What should happen if the boy keeps teasing Harsha even after he says stop?
qa.a: Harsha should not handle it alone; adults like the class teacher need to step in, as the teacher already did that afternoon.

qa.q: How might the ruler boy have felt when Harsha spoke up?
qa.a: He was probably taken by surprise, since he stood there with his mouth open and had expected Harsha to freeze.

grounding: A classmate watches a child who practised a calm, firm voice say stop and leave, with adults still involved.

passage:
Monday. Naveen finally told his class teacher that Tarun had been flicking his ears every day in the queue. She listened and said she'd watch the queue closely.
Tuesday. At home, Naveen practised in the mirror with Amma. "Stop that. I don't like it." At first his voice wobbled. By the tenth try, it was calm and firm, and he stood taller.
Thursday. In the queue, Tarun reached for his ear. Naveen turned, looked him in the eye and said, "Stop that. I don't like it." Then he walked to the front of the line. His knees shook, but he did it.
Tarun tried again at lunch. This time the class teacher stepped in herself.

qa.q: Where did Tarun flick Naveen's ears?
How did Naveen feel when he spoke up on Thursday?
qa.a: He felt nervous, with shaking knees, but also brave and proud that he said it calmly and walked away.

qa.q: Why did practising with Amma help?
qa.a: Repeating the words in the mirror made Naveen's voice calm and firm, so on the day he could say them without freezing.

qa.q: How might the class teacher see her role when Tarun tried again?
qa.a: She sees that Naveen shouldn't handle it alone, so she steps in herself once Tarun keeps going.

grounding: After telling an adult and practising a calm firm voice, a boy tells the bully to stop and walks away; when it continues, the teacher steps in.

passage:
"Chetan, your Gopika Ammamma was scared once too. When I was eleven, a girl called Kanaka hid my chappals every day during prayer, so I walked home barefoot on hot stones.
I finally told my teacher, and she said, 'Practise saying stop.' So every night I stood in front of my mother and said, 'Stop that. I don't like it.' My mother made me say it louder until my voice didn't shake.
One day Kanaka came for my chappals. I said it, just like that, and walked away. She stood there with her mouth open.
She tried once more the next week. That time the teacher stood beside me and dealt with her. I never had to face her alone again."

qa.q: What did Kanaka hide during prayer?
qa.a: Her chappals, which Kanaka hid every day during prayer.

qa.q: How did young Gopika feel walking home barefoot?
qa.a: She felt scared and helpless, suffering the hot stones because she didn't yet know how to stop Kanaka.

qa.q: What turning point in the story helped young Gopika?
qa.a: Telling the teacher and practising the words with her mother until her voice was steady, so she could say them and walk away.

qa.q: How might Kanaka have felt when Gopika spoke up?
qa.a: Kanaka seemed shocked and caught off guard, standing there with her mouth open.

grounding: A grandmother recalls telling a teacher, practising a calm firm voice and saying stop that and walking away; when it continued, the teacher stepped in.
